newsitem.title: USA: Gore pledges White House support for labor unions.
newsitem.headline: Gore pledges White House support for labor unions.

text.p: Pledging White House support for labour unions, Vice President Al Gore on Tuesday promised there would be a new look to the way the federal government does business with its contractors.
The way a company treats unions, he said, would weigh heavily in Washington's decisions to award them contracts.
"This White House will take action to give the right to organise (unions) new teeth," he told reporters after addressing the annual winter meeting of the executive council of the AFL-CIO.

In addition, Gore said, President Clinton's administration intends to take away tax benefits from government contractors who fight unions in court and try to dissuade employees from joining labour organisations.

"The president and I stand on the side of working men and women who want to exercise their right to unionize, so we're going to send a message to companies that want to do business with the federal government -- how you treat your employees and how you treat unions counts with us," Gore said.

He added that if companies wanted to do business with the federal government, "You'd better get your house in order and clean up your acts because today we're going to start changing the rules on federal contracting to make it clear that part of having the kind of integrity and business ethics and performance capability that we expect of a federal contractor is having a satisfactory record of labour relations and employment practices and policies."

"... If you want to do business with the federal government you had better maintain a safe workplace and respect ... union rights. That will be taken into account in decisions on federal contracting," Gore said.
He said the practice that federal contractors could be reimbursed for money they spend trying to convince employees not to join unions would come to an end.

Also ending, Gore said, was the practice that if companies are taken to court over allegations of unfair labour practices, "They have been able to use taxpayer money in order to pay the lawyers that fight against men and women who are simply trying to exercise their legitimate rights to organise.
"Today we're going to start changing those rules because they're just plain wrong," he added.
Gore said the right to organise and the right to strike were fundamental rights, "and nobody's tax dollars should be spent undermining those rights."

The vice president did not specify how the changes would be made, but delegates to the meeting of the American Federation of Labour and Congress of Industrial Organisations said it was "the cherry on the cake" for their annual conference.
Delegates were also courted by the two leading Democrats in Congress, House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt and Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle.
In separate press conferences, Gephardt and Gore clashed on the future role of NAFTA, the North American Free Trade Agreement, and how it had performed since its inception.
Gephardt, a strong foe of the treaty, said it had "not been an adequate force for progress."

Pointing out that wages in Mexican border towns had dropped from an average of about $1 an hour to 70 cents an hour, Gephardt told reporters, "So we're moving in the wrong direction, and in a way NAFTA has validated a system, a governmental and business system, that does not allow workers to have the ability to get paid and compensated for their hard work. Their productivity is way up, their wages are way down."

But Gore blamed the economic downturn in Mexico following that country's devaluation of the peso for NAFTA's apparent woes. He said if that factor was taken out of the equation, "The impact of NAFTA has been quite positive in Mexico and in the United States and Canada."

Chile has been mentioned as the next likely partner in the treaty through a proposed "fast track" agreement between Congress and the White House that would allow the Clinton administration to conclude a trade agreement with another country without it being altered by the legislators.

But Gephardt said there could be no fast track until NAFTA's current problems had been solved, and Daschle said the prospects of Chile joining NAFTA were "not very good," posing a problem for Clinton among his own party members.
